title: Absolute m-pseudo-coherence on schemes is closed under binary summands
statement: Let $Y$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme], let $m\in\mathbf Z$, and let $A,B\in D(\mathcal O_Y)$ [def-pc-derived-category]. If $A\oplus B$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent [def-sfb-m-pseudo-coherent-complex], then $A$ and $B$ are $m$-pseudo-coherent for that same integer $m$. No quasi-coherence, Noetherian hypothesis, or global cohomological boundedness is assumed.

source.place: Tag 08CE, lemma-summands-pseudo-coherent, fixed-m assertion, specialized to the ringed space of a scheme; definition Tag 08CB, definition-pseudo-coherent

proof.text: Work locally on a member $U$ of a covering carrying a strictly perfect approximation $P\to E|_U$, where $E=A\oplus B$. For the open immersion $j:U\to Y$ the ring map $j^{-1}\mathcal O_Y\to\mathcal O_U$ is the identity, so the derived pullback $Lj^*$ of the definition is the termwise restriction followed by the identity change of rings, i.e. the termwise restriction. Restriction is exact and its derived functor is computed termwise and is triangulated, so $E|_U=A|_U\oplus B|_U$; write these restrictions again as $E,A,B$. Exactness also preserves the approximation after any further restriction. Choose $N\ge m$ above every nonzero degree of $P$. Then $H^i(E)=0$ for $i>N$. The inclusion and projection of each summand compose to its identity; applying $H^i$ makes each $H^i(A)$ and $H^i(B)$ a retract of zero for $i>N$, hence zero. This bound is chosen separately on each $U$. On the site of opens of $U$, module sheaves and their restrictions are precisely the usual ones. The ringed-site approximation condition agrees with the scheme condition: restrict a covering of $U$ to any open $V$ by intersections, and conversely take the site object $U$. Thus the cited ringed-site triangle theorem applies to this scheme definition.

Two elementary consequences of the approximation definition will be used. If $T$ is $a$-pseudo-coherent and $b\ge a$, the same approximation is an isomorphism above $b$ and a surjection at $b$ (at $b>a$ it is even an isomorphism), so $T$ is $b$-pseudo-coherent. For any integer $r$, shift an approximation by $r$: its cohomology in degree $i$ is the old cohomology in degree $i+r$, since the shifted differential is $(-1)^r d$. The shifted complex remains strictly perfect. Consequently $T[r]$ is $a$-pseudo-coherent exactly when $T$ is $(a+r)$-pseudo-coherent. Composing an approximation with an isomorphism also preserves its properties.

Take the identity distinguished triangle $A\xrightarrow{1}A\to0\to A[1]$. The zero chain map on a representative of $B$ has cone $B\oplus B[1]$ with differential $\operatorname{diag}(d_B,-d_B)$, so its cone triangle is $B\xrightarrow{0}B\to B\oplus B[1]\to B[1]$. The finite-sum triangle theorem, for the two-element index set, gives a distinguished triangle $E\xrightarrow{1_A\oplus0}E\to C\to E[1]$, where $C=B\oplus B[1]$ and the zero summand in its third vertex has been removed by the canonical isomorphism.

The first $E$ is $(m+1)$-pseudo-coherent by step 2 and the second is $m$-pseudo-coherent by hypothesis. Apply clause (1) of the ringed-site triangle theorem to step 3: $C=B\oplus B[1]$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent. For every integer $t\ge0$, step 2 makes $C$ $(m+t)$-pseudo-coherent, hence $C[t]=B[t]\oplus B[t+1]$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent. The displayed biproduct identification holds because shift is additive.

Choose an integer $n\ge1$ with $m+n>N$, using the local bound from step 1. For every $i\ge m$, $H^i(B[n])=H^{i+n}(B)=0$. The unique map from the zero strictly perfect complex to $B[n]$ is therefore an isomorphism above $m$ and surjective at $m$. It witnesses that $B[n]$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent, starting a finite downward induction.

Suppose $1\le j\le n$ and $B[j]$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent. The split-triangle lemma gives the distinguished triangle $B[j]\to B[j]\oplus B[j-1]\to B[j-1]\to B[j+1]$. Its first term is $(m+1)$-pseudo-coherent by step 2. Its middle term is isomorphic, by exchanging the summands, to $C[j-1]$, which is $m$-pseudo-coherent by step 4 since $j-1\ge0$. Clause (1) of the ringed-site triangle theorem therefore makes $B[j-1]$ $m$-pseudo-coherent. Starting at $j=n$ and successively taking $j=n-1,\ldots,1$ proves the assertion for $B=B[0]$.

Interchange $A$ and $B$ in steps 3--6, using $B\oplus A\cong E$ and the bound for $A$ from step 1, to obtain $m$-pseudo-coherence of $A$ on $U$ as well. Do this on every member $U$ of the initial covering. For each summand, the local approximation coverings on the $U$ together form an open covering of $Y$, with the same integer $m$; these approximations are exactly the witnesses in the definition on $Y$. This proves both conclusions. If $Y$ is empty the empty covering already witnesses both, and zero summands are included by the zero approximation.
